job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Carlos Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mate, my days are a bit of a mix. I'm up early, then I do job applications with an AI assistant helping me tailor each one. Afternoons I work on my side project, a small service that automates bookkeeping for tradies, plumbers and sparkies who hate paperwork. I share a room in a house in Footscray with my cousin Mateo. I finished a commerce degree in finance and information systems at Monash with a top result, and I did internships at a fintech and a logistics company. No offer yet, but I've had three final-round interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, and that the people who lost money on hype will be loud about it. I'd tell my mates it's a good tool and a bad religion. And I'd keep using it every day, because it still saves me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fine. My plan doesn't depend on a revolution, it depends on small savings in boring places, like tradies' invoices. The openings round here are plentiful, and I've been in three final rounds. I think one lands soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, keep building the side project, and sign up two more tradies as test customers. I've got over six months in the bank and no debt, so I can afford to be picky. I'd be looking for a job where I can also use the side project's ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. I'm 23, I've got something I'm building, and a few interviews. I'd say I'm calm and a bit impatient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one pressure in your life right now that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting for a yes. The third final round was last week and they said two weeks. I know I should stop refreshing my email. My mum, who cleans offices at night, keeps asking and I keep saying soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you talk to about the job search, and what would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Mateo, who's an apprentice sparky, and a mentor at the fintech called Ruth. Mateo tells me which tradies are the worst at paperwork. Ruth tells me not to quit the job search for the project. They both give useful, different advice.

I'd tell mates people who lost money on **hype** will be loud.

do: Keep applying for jobs and **building** the side project every afternoon.
Sign up **two more tradies** as test customers.
feel: **Calm** and a bit impatient, with something I'm building and interviews lined up.

steps.text: Apply to jobs that could use his bookkeeping automation ideas
Sign up two more tradies as test customers
Keep using the AI assistant for tailoring each application

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the new normal and it's going to feel like a bumpy road. At work I'd say learn the tools or be stuck. Online I'd post about what I've built, and I'd say people shouldn't fear it too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the junior jobs I'm applying for change shape. The grunt work, reconciling, data entry, first-pass checking, gets done by tools. The firm would then hire fewer juniors, but better ones. I think I'm better placed than most, though I'd be lying if I said I wasn't a bit nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on my side project. It's the kind of thing that grows when small businesses want to automate. I'd take a job at a firm with a real analytics team and use it to learn. I'd also build a small online course for tradies on how to use the tools for invoicing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. Looking for work in this market feels like surfing. If you read the waves it's fun, but I know some people wipe out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry-level tasks in your field would go first, and what does that do to a job like the one you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first things are the plain jobs like invoice matching and tax prep checks. The firm I interned at already did that with software, and the three juniors were doing the review. The review part stays, and that's where I'd aim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who graduated a year after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the safe thing is no longer the safe thing. Go build something, even small, and learn how the tools work. And take one customer-facing job, because that's the part that won't vanish soon.

say: I'd say it's the **new normal** and learn the tools or get stuck.

fieldNote: He expects **fewer junior jobs** but feels ready.
Uses a **side project** as a hedge against the job market.
Thinks in terms of customer-facing roles as safer.

steps.text: Build an online course for tradies on invoicing automation
Take a job at a firm with a real analytics team
Keep testing new AI tools at work every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hold on, the world's about to change and we need a plan. I'd write something long and public. I'd also say to my mates that we should look after each other, because it's going to hit hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a bit sick. If AI does nearly all thinking work as well as me, my side project has competition from the big players too. The bookkeeping idea might be wiped out. But tradies still need a person they trust, and I think I can be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up everything. Close the first small customers, and ask if I can run the service as a local business with my cousin's apprenticeship contacts. I'd also take any decent job to have income. I'd keep three months in the bank and spend the rest on getting customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and I'd say a bit excited too. It's scary because of the speed, but I'd rather be a person doing something than one waiting for it to land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about how you spend the next few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly work on the side business, and talk to as many tradies as I can. I'd focus on being the trusted person, the one who turns up and explains. And I'd tell my mum to keep working for now, but to let me help with the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family the night this was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my mum and my cousin that I'm going to be okay, and I'd mean most of it. I'd say let's talk every Sunday so nobody's alone with it. I'd make a big dinner.

I'd tell mates to **look after each other**.

Tradies still need a **person they trust**, and I can be that person.

S2.quote: I'd rather be a person doing something than one waiting for it to land.
fieldNote: Bets that **trust with tradies** survives when software is free.
Plans a Sunday check-in with his mum and cousin.

steps.text: Close the first paying customers for the bookkeeping service
Take any decent job to keep income steady

Hold a Sunday family call so nobody copes alone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good warning and that we should treat it like a project. Five years to get the schools and the training right, and for people to learn the tools. I'd offer to run a free evening workshop for tradies on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good about it. Five years is enough to take a job, build my business into something and have a cushion. I'd see it as the window when I should do my biggest bets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take the job, build the business to five or ten customers, and put money into a property deposit with my cousin. I'd learn more about how the new tools work, because people will pay for someone who gets them. And I'd work on being the person who runs the tools, not just uses them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit buzzing. I feel more energy than fear, which I know is a privilege.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years it's a sprint. With five, I can run the business properly, and it's a long game. I'd probably hire one or two people, maybe Mateo's apprentice mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, or start doing, that you wouldn't if it were sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go bigger. I'd take more risk, because a cushion and a window are worth using. If it doesn't work out I'd have time to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and anyone panicking is wasting it. I'd say we should invest in people. I'd probably join a local group that helps small firms understand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, great. A decade is two careers' worth of experiments. I'd have time to build and sell a business, and to try a second one. The only thing is not to get comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take a good job, run the side project and try something bigger. Save, buy a place with my cousin by 26 or 27. And keep learning, with something new each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd be pretty excited, honestly. Ten years is a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set a goal to sell the business or scale it by 30. And I'd keep an eye out for the point where AGI actually appears, and be ready to jump. That's the beauty of having ten years, I'd get to see how it unfolds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you feel safe, or does it just push the worry further off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel safe, yes, though safe for me isn't safe for everyone. Mum cleans offices at night, and cleaning isn't going to be replaced in my first five years, but it will be after. That's what I'd worry about, helping her.

The only trap is getting **comfortable**, which I'd have to watch for.

S4.quote: A decade is two careers' worth of experiments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only one where being quick and keen might not be enough. What would help is a way for people with ideas to get a bit of funding fast, retraining for people who aren't tech-savvy, and honest talk from governments. I'd also like help making sure my mum has an income floor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume I'm confident because I use the tools. Honestly, it's because my mum worked nights so I could study. I feel I owe her something, and that's what drives me.

headlineQuote: My mum worked nights so I could study. I feel I owe her something, and that's what drives me.
portrait: Carlos is 23, a **top graduate** in finance and information systems from Monash, sharing a Footscray room with his cousin.
He uses AI tools every day and is building a **bookkeeping side project** for tradies.
Centre in his views, he sees change as **surfing**: fun if you read the waves.
He stays calm or uneasy in every world, and his deepest worry is his **mum's** income.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, where being quick might not be enough for people like his mum.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast funding** for people with ideas, retraining for the less tech-savvy, and an income floor for his mum.
